turns.text: A clang, metal on metal, three floors down and gone before the echo finishes deciding which way to bend. Whiskers read the silence after it as worse than the sound itself. Body stays exactly where it is — wedged between a coolant pipe and cold steel — waiting to see what a stopped noise decides to do next.

the shaft runs the full height of the tower's service core, a black throat of ladder-rungs and conduit, air thick with machine-oil and the ozone tang of something upstream working too hard. the clang doesn't repeat — just a maintenance drone dropping a tool three landings up, already forgotten by whatever's operating it. red emergency lighting bleeds down the walls in slow pulses, the only rhythm this shaft keeps. somewhere below, an elevator car groans against its cable, patient, waiting for a call nobody's making tonight.

Paws test the first rung before trusting it, claws finding purchase in rust rather than paint. The oil-smell pulls one way, the ozone pulls another — hunger votes for oil, caution votes for neither. Climbs down anyway, slow, keeping the pipe between body and open shaft the whole descent.

two landings down, a maintenance alcove opens off the shaft — a bolted stool, a coffee-ring table nobody's wiped in months, and a mini-fridge unit humming its own small heartbeat in the dark. its display cycles slow: COMPATIBILITY: 94%. MISS YOU ALREADY. nobody's opened that door in a long time, but the fridge keeps talking anyway, devoted to whoever it last matched with, whether or not they're ever coming back for it.

Fridge-hum gets a slow blink and nothing else — that particular loneliness doesn't smell like food, so it isn't tonight's problem. Nose drops to the table's edge instead, chasing a coffee-ghost smell that's older than useful.

below the alcove the shaft narrows around a service elevator's roof — car stopped mid-travel, cable slack in a way cables aren't supposed to go slack, a maintenance placard swinging on one screw: OUT OF SERVICE — DO NOT BOARD. dust sits undisturbed across the whole roof except for one clean paw-sized patch near the hatch, already there before you arrived.

Paw finds the clean patch first, then the nose — a foil wrapper wedged into the hatch seam, chewed at one corner by teeth that got here first. Under the food-smell that isn't food is something stranger: a taste that isn't a taste, copper and radio-hiss, worming up through the tongue from nowhere teeth can reach.

the wrapper reads NEURAL PATCH — FIELD TEST — VOLUNTEERS ONLY in corporate sans-serif, chewed edge curling where somebody's molars decided testing meant tasting. whatever's left inside it was never meant for a cat's mouth, but the shaft doesn't stop that from happening to somebody, one desperate meal at a time. the hatch under it groans faintly, metal remembering the weight of whoever stood here before.

That taste gets spat clean off the tongue in three hard head-shakes, nothing about it worth a second bite. Weight shifts off the hatch fast, back onto the ladder rungs — an elevator's slack cable is one more thing this body doesn't trust with its full weight.

the retreat's barely finished when the cable takes up slack all at once — the car lurching half a meter down the shaft with a shriek of old brake-clamp, dust raining off every landing at once. two floors up, a maintenance-alert light flips from standby to active red, and something with rotors starts climbing the shaft to investigate its own alarm.

Ladder rungs blur past too fast to count individually, claws barely tagging every third one, aiming for the alcove's dark instead of the open shaft the rotor-whine is climbing straight up. Flattens down behind the humming fridge, breath held, every rung-clang from below sounding closer than it probably is.

the drone noses into the alcove's mouth, downlight sweeping stool, table, coffee-ring — and the fridge, still cycling MISS YOU ALREADY into the red light like it's got somewhere better to be. the beam holds on the fridge a half-second too long, decides warm mini-compressor hum reads as hardware and not threat, and pulls back out into the shaft, climbing on past without slowing.

Air goes back into the lungs slow, not trusting the quiet yet to actually be quiet. Waits three full breaths past when the rotor-whine fades before uncurling from behind the fridge, already angling toward a side vent instead of the ladder — one alarm is enough education for tonight.

the side vent is narrow, dust-caked, angled down toward a grate that lets out onto a service alley three stories below tower-level — cold air pouring up through it, carrying real weather instead of shaft-recycled air, rain-smell and traffic-hum and the ordinary indifferent city instead of the tower's held-breath quiet.

Claws hook the vent's ribs one at a time on the way down, controlled, unhurried now that the shaft's noise is a floor away and shrinking. The grate at the bottom gives on the second push. Alley air replaces tower air in one full breath, and the whole body relaxes half a degree it didn't know it was holding.

the service alley runs behind the arcology's loading bays, dumpster-steam and wet asphalt, a string of motion-lights clicking on and off along the wall in a lazy uneven relay as something small moves under them. two bins down, a torn NEKOCORP snack pouch lies split open, most of its contents already gone to somebody faster, but a scatter of dry kibble still freckles the wet ground around it.

Nose confirms it before the eyes bother — real enough, cheap enough, still food. Works through the scatter piece by piece, ears swiveling between bites, one eye always on the alley's open end in case tonight's luck is only borrowed.

the motion-lights settle into their slow relay, click and dark and click again, and the loading bay's shutter groans down another notch on its automatic timer, sealing the tower's ground floor off from a night it was never built to acknowledge. rain starts up thin overhead, more mist than weather, softening every hard edge the alley has left.

Last of the kibble goes down without ceremony. Finds the gap between two dumpsters, dry enough, narrow enough to defend, and folds down into it — the fridge's small devoted hum, the wrapper's wrong copper taste, the rotor-whine climbing an empty shaft, all of it filed away for whatever tomorrow decides to make of it.

the tower keeps its red pulse going somewhere far up in the dark, patient, unbothered, one more alarm already resolved and logged and forgotten by whatever logs these things. down at street level the mist keeps falling on dumpsters and asphalt alike, and one small shape breathes even and slow in the gap between them, fed enough, dry enough, ears still working.
